startup.name: Gamgee
startup.description: Gamgee runs an end to end service for personalised mRNA cancer vaccines for dogs: sequence tumour and healthy DNA, find tumour specific mutations, design a vaccine, and manage vet intake, production, treatment and monitoring. Owners and vets pay per case. Early clinical trials in Australia. Team of 2, Summer 2026 batch.

yc_acceptance.basis: Test assumes the company was accepted, so this is only a note. Prior about 1 percent (0.6 to 2 percent third party range). Up for a vivid personal origin and a technical founder story with a real treated case, down for biotech capital need, a regulatory path that YC rarely funds and a team of only two.
yc_acceptance.why_it_fails: YC would most plausibly pass because one treated dog is not a repeatable business: the evidence is a single case, the vaccine was made with university scientists and the founder's wet lab and veterinary credentials are unclear. Biotech with long timelines is also a poor fit for a three month batch.

anchors.adjustment_reason: 0.74 times the 0.74 anchor, near the 0.75 floor. The anchor counts any seed ever and healthcare is slow (about 11 months median to seed), while this test needs a round above $500K within roughly 12 months. The viral origin story and AI angle raise it, regulated biotech and two founders lower it.

bands.rationale: Thin round of angels or grants just above the standard deal; biotech seeds often start small as in LEAH Labs which lived on grants and small angel money.
Typical bio seed of $2 to 5M, similar to FidoCure's $5M seed from a bio fund in 2019.
Upside if the viral story and trial data bring a bio fund to lead.

ladder.why_it_fails: The seed stalls if investors see one treated dog as an anecdote and the company cannot show a second and third case, or a credible cost per vaccine. Bio funds want a clear regulatory pathway with the animal drug regulator, and vet oncologists must refer cases. LEAH Labs lived on grants for years without a priced round, and Immunity Project never raised.

ladder.why_it_fails: A Series A needs controlled trial data showing response and a manufacturing process that turns around a vaccine at a cost owners can pay, around thousands of dollars. Individual mRNA design is expensive and each case is a new drug. FidoCure reached an A with a standing sequencing and drug matching model, but Helix Nanotechnologies, a similar mRNA platform, raised nothing found in years.

FidoCure stopped at a Series A and Adventris, which is human, is still preclinical.

ladder.why_it_fails: A Series C needs a pivot into human oncology or a profitable large veterinary business. The regulatory costs, trial sizes and mRNA manufacturing required are large, and the company might be acquired by an animal health major before then. Nuntius and Sensible show how long mRNA platforms take.

outcomes.why_it_fails: Most likely it stalls as a one off service that cannot scale because each vaccine is custom and veterinary demand is small, or it is acquired for its data and team. Helix Nanotechnologies and Immunity Project stayed active without large rounds, and VetPronto sold for a small amount. A billion dollar outcome requires human oncology success, which is a different company.

killers.risk: One case does not generalise and trials show no consistent benefit
killers.evidence: The company's proof is a single dog; tumour response to personalised vaccines is variable and unproven in controlled settings.
killers.mitigation: Run a registered trial with matched controls and publish the results.

killers.risk: Unit economics fail because each custom vaccine costs more than owners will pay
killers.evidence: Sequencing, design and mRNA production per patient cost thousands and the companion animal market has a spending ceiling.
killers.mitigation: Standardise manufacturing, batch cases and start with owners who accept premium prices.

killers.risk: Regulatory and manufacturing limits slow growth and need capital the seed will not cover
killers.evidence: Animal biologics need approvals and GMP like production, and the founder works through university labs.
killers.mitigation: Partner with a contract manufacturer and the regulator early and use non dilutive grants.

technical_complexity.rationale: The work spans genomics, computational vaccine design, mRNA manufacturing and clinical validation, which a two person team cannot do alone. The hard parts are partly solvable through partners and labs, but they set the timeline and cost. Model assisted target discovery is the easy part.

takeover_risk.rationale: Large animal health firms have the distribution but not a personalised mRNA service, and building one needs years of trials. A funded rival like FidoCure or Torigen could add mRNA in a few years, so risk is moderate.

evidence.claim: Cancer is a leading cause of death in dogs and owners spend heavily on treatment, with existing paid canine immunotherapy products.
FidoCure showed that dog owners pay for genomic cancer treatment and that funds back the category.

brand.name: Gamgee
brand.name_check: python3 -I scripts/name_features.py --score "Gamgee" --era 2022+: invented or proper noun, 6 characters, 1 word
strengths: Warm literary reference to a loyal companion that suits pets
weaknesses: Name says nothing about medicine, so trust must come from results
brand.rationale: A short, warm name fits the dog story and consumer owner trust, and short names did better in older YC eras. Companies like FidoCure used descriptive names, so Gamgee is more brand driven but credibility for a biotech still needs proof.

narrative.headline: A moving origin story and a real paid niche, but a custom biologic with one case of evidence and a heavy capital path.
narrative.general_summary: Gamgee turns one dog's treatment into a service for personalised mRNA vaccines for pets. Dog owners pay for cancer care and FidoCure shows investors fund the category, so a small seed is plausible, helped by a strong story. The hard parts are repeatable results, per case cost, regulation and manufacturing, and a Series A needs trial data. Analogs split between FidoCure, which raised an A, and mRNA or grant funded companies that stayed small. The healthcare cohort is slow to seed, so the one year seed estimate is lower than the cohort anchor.
